posts.title: Ohio 12-point suspension: how long it lasts and the four things you must do to get your license back
posts.description: Twelve points in two years is a six-month suspension in Ohio. Reinstatement takes a remedial course, a full exam retake, an SR-22 and a fee. Here is the order to do them in.

faq.q: How long is an Ohio 12-point suspension?
faq.a: Six months, for a driver who accumulates twelve or more points within a two-year period.

faq.q: Can I take the remedial course during the suspension?
faq.a: Yes. The course is online and does not require a valid license. Most drivers finish it during the suspension so the certificate is ready on reinstatement day.

faq.q: How long do I need an SR-22 after a 12-point suspension?
faq.a: The BMV's current guidance is one year for suspensions with a start date after April 9, 2025, and three years for earlier suspensions. Your suspension notice states your period.

posts.content:
**Short answer:** If you accumulate twelve or more points on your Ohio record within two years, the BMV suspends your license for six months. To get it back you have to do four things: complete an approved remedial driving course, retake the complete driver license exam, have your insurer file an SR-22 with the BMV, and pay a reinstatement fee. You can do the first one from your couch, during the suspension, and you should do it first.

## How you got here

Ohio assigns points to moving-violation convictions under Revised Code 4510.036. Most violations are two points. Speeding more than 30 mph over the limit, reckless operation and driving with a prohibited blood-alcohol level are four. OVI, fleeing an officer, street racing, leaving the scene and driving under a twelve-point suspension are six. The BMV sends a warning letter when you reach six points in a two-year window, listing every violation and its points. Twelve or more in that window and the suspension letter follows.

The two-year window is measured from the dates of the violations, not the convictions, so a ticket you paid last month for something that happened eighteen months ago still counts.

## How long the suspension lasts

Six months. The BMV's twelve-point suspension page says it plainly: "Serve six-month suspension." Some drivers qualify for limited driving privileges during that period; that is a request to the court, not the BMV, and it is separate from reinstatement.

## The four reinstatement requirements, in the right order

### 1. Complete a remedial driving course (do this first)

Ohio law requires an approved adult remedial driving course before reinstatement. It is eight hours of measured instruction with a forty-question final exam passed at 75%. It is entirely online, so you do not need a valid license to take it, and you can finish it while the suspension is running. Do it early: Ohio gives you thirty days from the moment you start the content to finish, and the exam allows one retake, twenty-four hours after a failed attempt.

[Our Ohio remedial course](/ohio) is $69.95 with the certificate included. Whichever provider you choose, make sure it appears on the Ohio Department of Public Safety's list of approved remedial schools, because a certificate from an unapproved course does not count.

### 2. Retake the complete driver license exam

This is not the remedial course's exam. It is the BMV's own knowledge test and driving test, the same ones a new driver takes. Schedule it for after your suspension ends; the remedial course is good preparation because its content is drawn from the same traffic-law material.

### 3. File proof of financial responsibility (an SR-22)

An SR-22 is not a type of insurance. It is a form your insurer files with the BMV certifying that you carry at least Ohio's minimum liability coverage. The BMV's current guidance is that suspensions starting after April 9, 2025 carry a one-year filing requirement, and earlier suspensions carry three years. If the policy lapses during that period, the insurer notifies the BMV and the suspension can return.

### 4. Pay the reinstatement fee

Paid to the BMV, online or in person, once the other three are done. The amount is on the BMV's reinstatement fee schedule and in your suspension notice.

## A note on the two-point credit

You may read that the remedial course "gives you two points back." That is a different program, for drivers with at least two but fewer than twelve points, and it does not apply once you have been suspended. Completing the course as a reinstatement requirement does not remove any points from your record. What it does is satisfy one of the four conditions the BMV set.

## What to do today

1. Pull your driving record from the BMV so you know the exact points and dates.
2. Enroll in an approved remedial course and finish it inside its thirty-day window.
3. Call your insurer about the SR-22 so it is ready to file the day your suspension ends.
4. Book the BMV exam for the first available date after the suspension period.

Do those in that order and reinstatement day is a fee and a signature, not a scramble.

posts.title: Does the Ohio remedial driving course remove points? What the two-point credit actually does
posts.description: No. Ohio's BMV says completion "does not remove points from your record." The two-point credit raises the suspension threshold instead. Here is exactly how it works and who qualifies.

faq.q: How many points does the Ohio remedial course credit?
faq.a: Two. The credit applies to drivers with at least two but fewer than twelve points, once every three years, up to five times in a lifetime.

faq.q: Does a court-ordered remedial course earn the credit?
faq.a: No. Ohio Revised Code 4510.037 bars the registrar from approving a credit for a course completed under a judge's order.

faq.q: Will the credit hide my violations from my insurer?
faq.a: No. The convictions and their points stay on your record. The credit changes the suspension math, not the record.

posts.content:
**Short answer:** No. The Ohio BMV's own page says completing a remedial driving course "does not remove points from your record, but can act as a cushion against future convictions that may take you to 12 points within a two-year period." What you get is a two-point credit, which changes when a twelve-point suspension is triggered. Your violations stay on the record.

## The rule, from the statute

Ohio Revised Code 4510.037 lets a driver who has at least two but fewer than twelve points complete an approved remedial driving course and apply to the BMV registrar for a two-point credit. Three limits apply:

- **Once every three years.** One credit per three-year period.
- **Five in a lifetime.** After five credits, no more.
- **Not for court-ordered courses.** If a judge ordered the course, the registrar may not approve a credit.

## What "credit" means in practice

Think of it as raising the ceiling rather than lowering the floor. With a two-point credit on file, a twelve-point suspension is not triggered until your points within the two-year window reach fourteen. Nothing on the record is erased. Insurers, employers and courts see the same convictions they saw before.

That is still valuable. If you are sitting at eight or ten points with a year left in the window, two points of headroom is the difference between one more ticket being expensive and one more ticket being a six-month suspension.

## Who this is for, and who it is not for

**It is for you if** you have between two and eleven points, you have not used the credit in the last three years, and you want a margin.

**It is not for you if** you already have twelve or more points. At that point the course is a reinstatement requirement, not a credit, and completing it does not reduce the suspension. See our guide to [reinstating after a twelve-point suspension](/ohio/blog/ohio-12-point-suspension-how-to-get-your-license-back).

**It is also not for you if** a judge ordered the course. Take it, file the certificate, satisfy the order. Just know that no credit follows.

## What the course is

Eight hours of measured online instruction covering the nineteen topics Ohio requires, with knowledge checks after each unit and a forty-question final exam passed at 75%. Ohio gives you thirty days from the moment you start to finish. [Our course](/ohio) is $69.95 with the certificate included.

## How to apply for the credit

1. Complete the course and download your certificate.
2. Take it to the BMV or follow the submission instructions the BMV provides.
3. The registrar reviews your record and, if you are eligible, applies the credit.

Keep your certificate. The BMV can see completions entered through the state's DETS system, but a paper copy settles any question quickly.
